sections.h2: Recorder's Office location, hours and contact
sections.html:
The Marion County Recorder's Office is in the City-County Building, 200 E. Washington Street, Suite T-741, Indianapolis, IN 46204. The counter is open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday. The main number is 317.327.4020.

Phones are answered from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily, and a voicemail gets a callback within one to two business days. Email to recorder@indy.gov brings the fastest reply, so use it when your question can wait for a written answer.

This office is the permanent home of the county's property records: deeds, liens, mortgages, easements and survey maps, more than 11 million records in all. Since September 29, 2026 it no longer hands out forms or documents for recording. The reason given is protecting owners from property fraud, so a deed has to come from an attorney, a title company or your own preparation, not from the counter.

A deed gets stamped at the Assessor's Office first and then goes to the Recorder with the fee. The county's Record Your Deed page lays out the order of steps, and they are worth following in sequence because the Recorder will not accept an unstamped deed.

  1. Collect the exact name of the current owner and the legal description. The Assessor's property report card or the current tax bill has both.
  2. Prepare the deed. The grantor is the person now on title, and the grantee is the person who will be listed as the new owner. An attorney is the county's recommendation.
  3. Sign it in front of a notary.
  4. Take or mail it to the Assessor for the transfer stamp, with a separate check or money order for each office.
  5. The Recorder records the deed and sends it back to you.
  6. Apply through the Marion County Auditor for any deductions you qualify for.

You can submit by mail, through an e-recording partner or in person. Electronic filing dominates: in November 2025 the office recorded 8,764 documents and 7,948 of them were e-recordings.

Two offices charge two sets of fees, and each wants its own payment. The Recorder takes $35.00 per document. The Assessor adds $10.00 per parcel per document for the transfer and $20.00 for each sales disclosure form.

ChargeAmountOffice
Recording fee for a deed$35.00 per documentRecorder
Transfer fee$10.00 per parcel per documentAssessor
Sales disclosure form$20.00 per form, if requiredAssessor
Copies of recorded documents$1 per page up to 11 by 17 inchesRecorder

State law, Indiana Code 36-2-7-10, sets a base fee of $25 for a deed and $55 for a mortgage. A county with a consolidated city can add an optional housing trust fee of $2.50 for the first page and $1 for each added page, an identification security fee of $2, and an optional affordable housing fee of up to $10. Plan around the county's published $35 and let the Recorder's fee schedule decide the total when your document runs long or has unusual features.

Oversized pages cost more: $25 for the first and $5 for each additional. Military discharge papers are recorded free.

The office rejects a deed that is missing a required statement or breaks a formatting rule. The county's requirements page cites the Indiana Code for each item:

  • Notarization (IC 32-21-2-3).
  • A statement under penalties of perjury that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers, plus the name of the person who prepared the instrument (IC 36-2-11-15).
  • Names of signers and witnesses printed identically throughout and typed under each signature (IC 36-2-11-16).
  • Two-inch top and bottom margins on the first and last pages for the recording stamp. Skip them and an extra page is added (IC 36-2-11-16.5).
  • A street address where tax statements should be mailed (IC 32-21-2-3).
  • For a power of attorney signing, the document number of the power of attorney next to the signature.

The notary's name has to match the commission and appear with the county of residence, the commission expiration date and the date of notarization. Seals on commissions issued or renewed after July 1, 2018 must also carry the words "notary public," "State of Indiana," "seal," and the seven-digit commission number.

To re-record a document you pay the original fee again and state the reason at the top of the page. Include a self-addressed stamped envelope with any paper return.

sections.h2: Transfer fees and the sales disclosure form
sections.html:
Marion County charges flat transfer fees at the Assessor, not a percentage transfer tax: $10 per parcel and $20 per sales disclosure form.

Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3 requires the parties to complete and sign a sales disclosure form before a conveyance document is filed with the county auditor. The Assessor checks the form for accuracy and completeness, approves it and returns it to a party for filing. The county asks you to prepare the form in the Properly system at forms.properlytaxes.com, then print and sign it.

Take the paperwork to Room W121. That counter stops processing at 4 p.m., takes cash, a check for the exact amount or a card, and adds a small charge on cards. Staff there cannot help draft a deed, so bring one that an attorney or title company prepared.

Marion County residents can sign up free for the Property Fraud Alert service that the Recorder promotes, at propertyfraudalert.com/INMARION. It sends a notice when a document is recorded against your property, which gives you an early warning if someone files a forged deed.

An inherited house or one that sits empty is the sort of property worth signing up. The same fraud concern led the office to stop supplying blank recording forms.

The Recorder also offers a survivorship affidavit to remove a deceased owner from title, copies of deeds, a claim form for a recording fee refund and online search of real estate records.

Sellers rarely record anything themselves, because the title or escrow company arranges the stamp and the recording. Knowing the steps helps you spot the usual causes of delay:

  • A missing notary detail, or a name that differs from the vested deed.
  • A legal description that does not match the records.
  • A deed submitted without the Assessor stamp.
  • An unreleased mortgage or lien that still appears in the Recorder's index.

Title work on an older house can reach back through many owners, so check the chain of title early and ask the title company to flag gaps before you set a closing date. If you are weighing a quick sale of a house with title questions, a written cash offer lets you read the terms and the closing timeline before you commit to anything.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal, but it does not skip the Assessor stamp, the sales disclosure or the recording fee. Ask who pays each charge when you review the contract, and have that written down so the closing statement holds no surprises.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Marion County?
faqs.a: The Recorder charges $35.00 per document. The Assessor charges separately: $10.00 per parcel per document, and $20.00 for each sales disclosure when one is required.

faqs.q: Do I record a deed before or after the Assessor stamps it?
faqs.a: After. The Assessor's transfer stamp comes first, and then you take the stamped deed to the Recorder in Room T-741.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Marion County?
faqs.a: Yes. The office accepts documents by mail, through e-recording partners or in person, and most of what it records now arrives electronically.

faqs.q: Does the Marion County Recorder hand out deed forms?
faqs.a: No. Since September 29, 2026 the office no longer provides forms or documents for recording, so have an attorney or title company draft the deed.

faqs.q: Is there a percentage transfer tax in Marion County?
faqs.a: No. The county lists flat fees: $10 per parcel for the transfer and $20 per sales disclosure at the Assessor, plus the Recorder's fee. Your title company can confirm the total for your sale.
